title: Word for the Same Day
attribution_note: Translated for this edition from the Russian of St Tikhon of Zadonsk (public domain), from the Words Spoken to the Voronezh Flock — the twelve long sermons he preached as bishop of Voronezh, 1763–1767. The Russian text the translation was made from is kept in the repository. A second sermon for the same feast, known in earlier editions by its opening text, 'See then that you walk circumspectly.'

pairs.en: *“See then that you walk circumspectly”* [Ephesians 5:15].

sections.heading: The man on a trembling throne

pairs.en: Picture a man seated upon a richly adorned throne, holding in his hands every pleasure — and yet, beneath him, he sees a fire kindling; above his head, a razor-sharp sword hanging by the thinnest of threads; and on every side, enemies arming themselves against him.

Judge for yourselves, my hearers: in such danger, in such terror, could all these pleasures and delights give this man any peace? Death surrounds him on every side — death above, death below, death on every hand. Would not such danger and such dread overwhelm every pleasure he possesses?

When I paint this picture of a man's condition, I am describing the condition of our own life. All of us who live upon the earth stand in exactly the same danger as this man. I offer this present word to the glory of God, in honor of today's feast, so that all of us, surrounded as we are by such dangers, may learn to walk more carefully in this world — heeding the exhortation of the God-wise teacher, Saint Paul: *“See then that you walk circumspectly.”*

When we open the eyes of our understanding, my hearers, and look closely at the circumstances of our life, we will see beyond doubt that it resembles the condition of that man — and that no beauty this world offers can truly delight us.

Above us we will see God, threatening us with the sword of His justice. Beneath us we will see the pit of hell, prepared for sinners. Behind us we will see our own sins, ceaselessly tormenting our conscience. Before us we will see death, drawing nearer to us without pause. To our right and to our left we will see the enemies of our souls, plotting against us and seeking our ruin.

God, who is above us, is almighty, so that none can stand against Him. He is our Creator and our Lord, who made us as a potter makes vessels of clay, and who can shatter us in a single moment — and therefore He is to be feared. For this reason Christ Himself commands us to fear Him: *“Fear Him who is able to destroy both soul and body in hell”* [Matthew 10:28]. And Jeremiah cries out to Him: *“Who would not fear You, O King of the nations?”* [Jeremiah 10:7]. He is also all-seeing, watching over all our deeds, all our designs, all the thoughts of our hearts. He sees even what we have not yet done: *“Your eyes saw my unformed substance,”* says the Psalmist [Psalm 139:16].

And since He is infinite Goodness, He hates even the smallest evil, and punishes it, for He is just. Among all the sons of Israel who came out of Egypt, none was dearer or more beloved to Him than holy Moses, with whom He spoke as a friend speaks with a friend, and for whose intercession He turned back the sword of His wrath from a rebellious and stiff-necked people — Moses, to whom He declared at last, *“I know you above all others”* [Exodus 33:12]. And yet, even him, God punished for a single transgression: He did not allow him to enter the promised land, though Moses longed for it with all his heart.

But if God punishes even His friends for a single transgression, what do you suppose will happen to you — you who dare, fearlessly and openly, to defy the law of God? You who lawlessly touch another man's marriage bed; you who shed a brother's blood; you who wrong your neighbor, secretly or openly; you who drink the bitter tears of widows, orphans, and the poor; you who devour without payment the labor of your workers and hired servants; you who touch with blaspheming lips the One who sits enthroned in heaven; you who break your oaths and your sworn word; you who, for some small and wounding word that grieved you, seek to wipe a man from the land of the living — and all sinners like you — what do you think will become of you?

Do you imagine you will escape the righteous judgment of God? Will your great transgressions go unpunished, when in the saints even small ones are punished? God punishes what is small — will He overlook what is great? *“Is there unrighteousness with God?* *Certainly not!”* [Romans 9:14]. Let it never even be thought — for *“the Lord is righteous, and there is no unrighteousness in Him”* [Psalm 92:15]. How many iniquities you keep adding to iniquity, how much wrath and fury of God you are storing up for yourselves, unless you quickly take refuge in God's mercy with repentance and broken tears! See, my hearers, what a sword hangs over us — the sword of God's justice, sharpened by our own sins.

But look now with the eye of the mind downward, and you will see beneath you a deep pit, hell gaping open, eager to devour sinners — and it would devour them at once, were it not restrained by God's mercy, by God's goodness, which waits for the sinner's repentance. This abyss is fearful even to holy men. Saint Cyril of Alexandria says: *“I fear Gehenna, for it is endless.* *I fear Tartarus, for it knows no warmth.* *I fear the darkness, for it knows no light.”* The other saints felt the very same fear. For the saints of God, who spent their whole lives in such repentance, who served God so faithfully that they feared to break even His smallest commandment, still trembled and dreaded that abyss. Shall we, then — sinners that we are — be without fear?

Saint John Chrysostom compares such fearless people to small children who are frightened by masks or costumes, but are not afraid of fire — so that they reach out and grasp it with their hands and are burned. So it is with people of childish understanding: they fear temporary misfortune, temporary troubles, chains, prison, poverty — all of which are sent by God, for the most part, to correct us — yet they do not tremble before Gehenna, which even the demons themselves dread, as the holy Gospel teaches: *“And they begged Him”* — that is, Christ — *“that He would not command them to go out into the abyss”* [Luke 8:31], though that abyss is prepared for them. In this we see the second danger — the one beneath us.

And when we look ahead, we will see a danger no less great: we will see death, which spares no one. The longer we live, the nearer it draws to us. This appointed boundary of God is as unknown to us as it is terrible. Unknown, because it snatches away the old and the young, infants and youths, the ready and the unready, the righteous and the sinful, without distinction. Terrible, because from that point begins an endless, unbroken, everlasting eternity. From there we pass either into eternal blessedness or eternal torment, into a place of joy or a place of weeping. At that moment we begin either to live forever or to die forever — to reign forever in heaven with Christ and His saints, or to suffer forever in hell with satan and his angels.

O death, death! How fearful is even the thought of you! Yet here is a strange thing: this inescapable fate awaits every one of us, and yet we live as though it did not exist. What wretched blindness is ours! Everyone knows the condition of a man who has been bound in irons, thrown into prison, and condemned to death. He no longer needs house or wife, children, friends, relatives, or riches. Food and drink no longer enter his mind. He has only one thought: that he is condemned to death, and awaits it. Possessed by this one fear alone, he grieves, laments, is broken in spirit, and waits for the day, the hour, when he must die.

The righteous judgment of God, back in Paradise, already condemned all of us, together with our forefather, to death: *“you are dust, and to dust you shall return”* [Genesis 3:19]. However many centuries have passed since then, no one has ever escaped that sentence — and the examples we see every day confirm it. Why, then, do we not live as men condemned to death? Why do we not fear that hour? Why do we not prepare for it? Why do we spend ourselves instead on banquets, drunkenness, luxury, games, amusements, and cards? Why do we wrong, rob, and deceive one another? Why do we delight in bows and flatteries, devised by the devil's own cunning? Why do we gather wealth through unrighteous gain, as though we would never have to part with it? Why, my hearers, do we feel nothing?

For we have been condemned to death by the judgment of God, just as surely as a man sitting in prison, and when the appointed time comes, the judgment of God will most certainly lead us out of the prison of this body, and dust will be given back to dust: *“you are dust, and to dust you shall go!”* Perhaps someone will object that this is not the same kind of death — that for a prisoner, death is forced and shameful, while for the rest of us it is an ordinary thing, coming through some unbearable illness.

But God alone knows what your own end will be — yes, yours, you who reason this way. Have you received some revelation from God as to how He has appointed your life to end? Perhaps you too will be put to death by execution. Perhaps you will drown in the depths of the sea, or be killed by robbers, or by treacherous men, or meet your end in some other such way. There are almost as many kinds of death as there are people in the world. We are all born in the same way, but we die in countless different ways. One man falls while standing and is dead in an instant. Another stumbles while walking and lies lifeless. Another leans over while sitting and is lifted up already dead. Another lies down to sleep at evening, and by morning is laid upon his deathbed. Another sits feasting and rejoicing at table, and in that very hour weeping takes the place of joy, and he is carried out to the grave amid lamentation. And whatever happens to another may happen to you, and to me. We are all people of the same nature, and subject to the same accidents. But when this will happen, we do not know. Therefore we must be ready for it at every hour.

But whenever and however our life comes to its end, it will not be without fear. For then the books of conscience will be opened for each of us. Then the deeds of each one will appear — the things he *“did while in the body, whether good or bad”* [2 Corinthians 5:10]. Then we will meet a trial we never once considered. Then two roads will appear before us: one leading to life, the other to eternal death. We must confess that the prince of darkness has blinded our eyes, so that we will not see that boundary appointed by God, nor think upon it — so that, thinking nothing of it, we go on carrying out his evil and destructive will, and so lose our salvation. This, my hearers, is what stands before us.

And when we look behind us, when we look with the eye of the mind, what will we see there? Ah, it is terrible even to glance in that direction! There stand our fierce adversaries, gripping us tightly, dragging us mercilessly before the Judge, striving to hand us over to eternal imprisonment. There, I say, are our sins — all those committed throughout our life — standing like monsters ready to fall upon us and cast us down to the bottom of hell. Our sins, I say, press in upon us, wound our conscience, and pierce it like a sword. These same merciless enemies cast the angels down from heaven to the bottom of hell and bound them with chains of darkness. These enemies drove our forefather Adam and all his descendants out of paradise. They brought the terrible flood upon the whole world. These enemies burned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah. These enemies struck down so many of God's people in the wilderness and kept them from entering the promised land. These same merciless enemies, even now, lay waste to cities and great kingdoms, shed so much blood, and bring on every other kind of calamity and disaster. Such, I say, are the fierce enemies that stand behind us and rise up against us.

sections.heading: Enemies to the right and left

pairs.en: But if we look about us still more carefully, and turn the eyes of our soul to the right and to the left, we will find no less danger there. On one side we will see the world with all its allurements; on the other, the prince of darkness with the principalities and powers of spiritual wickedness arming themselves against us. And so, when we turn aside from danger on one side, trouble comes upon us from the other.

Hear what Isaiah cries out concerning this: *“Fear, and the pit, and the snare are upon you who dwell on the earth.* *And it will be that he who flees from the fear shall fall into the pit, and he who climbs out of the pit shall be caught in the snare”* [Isaiah 24:17-18]. For, my hearers, just as wild beasts in the forest are hunted and caught by hunters, so people in this world are pursued and ensnared by the spirits of wickedness in the heavenly places. When a beast escapes the snare, it falls into a pit; and if it escapes the pit, it falls prey to the hounds. The same thing happens to a poor man. When he has freed himself from one scheme, he falls into another. He seeks solitude, and falls into a greater temptation, since satan attacks all the more fiercely in solitude. He abandons solitude and associates with neighbors, with corrupt friends, and is blackened by their malice as though by pitch. And should he live among them as Lot lived in Sodom, preserved by the grace of Christ, he immediately feels a violent assault of pride and self-conceit.

And so, wherever he turns, a snare of destruction lies before him. Saint Anthony the Great, as we read in church history, once saw the whole world, from earth to heaven, filled with snares, and cried out to the Lord with a sigh: *“Lord, who can be delivered from these snares?”* And indeed, no one could be delivered from them, were it not that the grace of God saves everyone.

Now, my hearers, weighing all these circumstances with the eyes of your understanding, judge for yourselves: is not our own life in exactly the same danger as that of the king's brother we spoke of at the beginning of this sermon? We see above our heads the sword of God's justice hanging over us. We see below us the open abyss of fiery Gehenna, prepared for sinners. We see before us death, drawing nearer to us hour by hour, seeking to seize us. We see behind us our sins, oppressing our conscience and piercing it, like a sword, with remembrance. We see on both sides the world and the devil, our enemies, hurling their arrows at us and wounding us.

And above all this, we sit upon a trembling throne of our own — our unstable nature, inclined to every kind of fall. Come now, brethren, I say to you: sitting on this trembling throne, surrounded by all these dangers, let us go ahead and clothe ourselves every day in purple and fine linen, like the rich man of the Gospel; let us invite our friends, fill our tables, adorn them with rich food, warm ourselves with sweet and costly wines, eat, feast, and make merry; let us order music to entertain us, arrange dances and masquerades; let us add operas too, when our money allows it. But will merriment even enter our minds? Will we want to celebrate, when fear surrounds us above and below, behind and before, and on both sides at once?

What, then, are we to do in such circumstances? How are we to be delivered from all these evils? Let us seek for ourselves a pattern by which we might escape these dangers. And here is the way that comes to mind: let us free ourselves from our sins through true and tearful repentance, which the merciful God has granted to us sinners because of our weakness. In this way we will free our conscience from their torment; through humble repentance we will turn away the righteous wrath of God, incline Him to mercy, and quench the Gehenna beneath us that our sins have kindled. For nothing moves the God who loves mankind so much as human tears, flowing from a broken heart.

We are urged and encouraged toward this by the Ninevites, who escaped the wrath of God through repentance. We are urged by Manasseh, king of Judah, who was freed from the bonds of sin through a broken heart. We are urged by the harlot, who washed Christ's feet with her tears, and so washed away the defilement of her sins. Saint Peter gives us the example — the chief apostle, who denied Christ three times, yet through bitter weeping was restored again to the company of the apostles. Let us imitate them, and turn with tender contrition to our Master. He, as a Father rich in mercy, inclining Himself toward compassion, will cleanse us from our sins, turn away His righteous wrath, and in His love for mankind deliver us from the abyss of hell.

And if God is reconciled with us, then death itself will no longer be fearsome to us. And we will be delivered from the other dangers as well — from the schemes of the devil and of the world — if we pray with tears to that same merciful God, our Provider, to open the eyes of our understanding, so that we may see the snares the enemy has spread out for us. And once we see them, by the grace of that same Lord we can turn aside from them; for the open attacks of the enemy are not as dangerous as the hidden ones, and are therefore easily avoided.

For help, protection, and shelter, let us always take refuge first in our Lady the Theotokos, the Advocate common to all Christians, whose holy Dormition we have celebrated today. Then let us earnestly call upon all the saints of God, that they may help us. For they, *“having themselves been tempted, are able to help us who are tempted”* [Hebrews 2:18]. Let us strive to imitate them in the carefulness of their lives. They turned aside from the enemy's schemes by keeping in mind the Four Last Things: death, judgment, hell, and the kingdom of heaven.

Let us take this to heart, and always keep death in mind. It will not let us boast of our noble birth, or look down on others, our own brethren. For in remembering death, we will remember that we are dust, and to dust we shall go. In remembering death, we will turn our hand away from extortion and theft, and will instead fill the hands of those who ask from our own possessions, knowing that everything worldly will remain to the world, and that just as we entered this world naked, so naked we shall leave it. In remembering death, we will not burden this bodily vessel with gluttony and drunkenness, but will take only as much food and drink as keeps us from growing weak and able to labor — remembering that we ourselves will soon be food for worms.

In remembering death, we will not covet costly and various garments, knowing that for burial nothing more is needed than a single shroud to cover our nakedness. In remembering death, we will not seize by cunning and wicked schemes whole villages, estates, and lands, knowing that after death no more than seven feet of earth will be needed for us.

So then, remembering death, let us keep great watchfulness to escape the enemy's schemes. And when we remember death, the Last Judgment will also come to mind — the judgment that follows death, at which we will be examined for every evil word, deed, and thought. So then, remembering death, let us also prepare for the Last Judgment, and strive by every means to appease the righteous Judge. For if, when we are summoned before a human court, we prepare how to conduct ourselves there, what to say, how to defend ourselves — how much more should we prepare for the judgment of God, at which all our very thoughts will be laid bare! At the Last Judgment two roads will present themselves to the mind: on the one, poor sinners go with weeping, wailing, and useless lamentation into eternal torment; on the other, blessed the righteous go with unspeakable joy into eternal life.

The constant remembrance of these Four Last Things will not allow us to be seduced by the sweetness of sin — as Scripture warns us, for our own safekeeping: *“Remember your Four Last Things, and you will never sin”* [Sirach 7:39]. Amen.
